P01.passage: A potter fired a batch of white bowls painted with blue brushwork under a clear glaze. The kiln's damper had stuck shut through the night, and the bowls came out smelling of smoke. The brushwork could no longer be seen through the glaze, and a damp cloth drawn across a bowl came away black. Under a fingertip the glaze was as smooth as glass, and a week later the bowls had held tea without a mark. In her notes on the batch, the potter concluded that the firing had ______ the glaze.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: In 1904 a new firm began making typewriters in a country where one older company had sold nearly every machine for thirty years, and by 1914 the newcomer was outselling it. Court records from 1912 show that three of the older company's draftsmen, who never left its payroll, had each received a monthly sum from the newcomer since 1905. The newcomer's machines reached the shops weeks before the older firm's matching models, sold through the same dealers. Reading both firms' records, one historian concluded that the newcomer had above all ______ its rival.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: Between the two world wars, exiles working for their small homeland's independence gathered at a café in a foreign capital, where the owner kept the back room for them. Each night the movement's nine-member committee sat at the long table, and no other exile was let into the room. Couriers left from the café for cells at home, letters came addressed to the owner, and the committee's files stayed in his safe. He turned foreign reporters away at the door, and all nine had led the movement since before the first war. In a memoir of those years, one journalist called the café, more than anything, the movement's ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. The road was raised on a bank through the middle of the town, between the mill and the streets where most of its workers lived. The school, the churches and the main street's forty stores stood on the mill side. Within a decade the streets beyond the bank had opened their own grocery, school and fire company, and by 1990 the town still had nearly eight thousand people. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: For five years of wartime occupation, a city's public library of some three hundred thousand volumes was under the control of the occupying authority. When the staff returned, the shelves of ordinary books stood full, and the locked room that had held the manuscripts and early printed books was bare. In the 1950s volumes bearing the library's stamp began turning up in the catalogs of three universities in the occupying country, which returned a few of them. In a postwar report, one librarian concluded that the occupation had ______ the library.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, icy bodies kept trickling inward from the belt's ragged inner edge, and nearly all of them crossed the giant's path and plunged into its clouds. The rocky planets were struck twenty times less often than in the run without the giant, and hardly any icy body left the system in either run. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. Each change met the treasury's needs of the moment, rising when revenue ran short and falling in years of surplus; seven were rises and four were cuts, and by 1950 the rate was four times its first level. Within two years of every change, the three neighboring countries had set their own duties to match, and traders in all four countries quoted wheat at the small country's rate. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: In 1897 gold was found in the hills above a small river town, and the rush lasted six years. Since river steamers had stopped calling in 1880, the town had shrunk from two thousand people to four hundred, and half its houses stood empty. Miners rented them through the rush, and when the gold gave out in 1903 many stayed to farm land left idle since the steamers stopped. By 1920 the town had nineteen hundred people, its main street still facing the river landing. Looking back in 1920, one historian wrote that the gold rush had ______ the town.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: In 1590 the council of a river city built a stone granary on its market square, large enough to hold a year's grain for every household. Each autumn the council filled it at whatever price the harvest set. Each spring it sold the grain to any buyer at one posted price, and over two centuries its accounts show neither profit nor loss. In that time the price of a loaf in the city swung less from year to year than in any town nearby. One economic historian has argued that for two centuries the granary served above all as the city's ______.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. The crews of small boats, who fished inshore at night, now waited hours on the quay for the auction, and within five years half of them had sold their boats for scrap and gone to work in the city's canneries. With fewer boats, a single stormy night could leave the auction with almost nothing to sell. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: In 1894 a court ruled on a strike by a port city's dockworkers' union, which then had four thousand members and a hall near the docks. The court let the union stand but forbade it to strike or to call a boycott. That week the members voted almost to a man to accept the ruling and make the union a benefit society, and over the next fifty years its membership grew to nine thousand, with a sick fund and a social hall. It never again stopped work on the docks. Writing fifty years later, one labor historian concluded that the ruling had, in effect, ______ the union.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: A single hawthorn hedge runs a mile east to west across open plowed fields between two oak woods, and voles burrow thickly in the bank beneath it. Collared females that dug into the bank in early spring were still there in late summer, and the young stoats that scattered from the hedge then were too small to have been collared in the spring. Through those months the females hunted in the oak woods at either end, crossing the open fields to reach them and back. After six years of tracking collared stoats there, one ecologist concluded that the animals used the hedge above all as their ______.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: A chalk quarry worked out in the 1800s lies at the edge of a market town, a pit two hundred yards across with galleries cut back into its walls. The galleries run half a mile into the hill under sixty feet of chalk. From 1940 to 1944 the town kept them lit and stocked with bedding, and its families slept in them on nights the sirens sounded. A spring-fed pond, clear to its gravel bed, covers the pit's floor from wall to wall. One local historian has called the quarry, above all, the town's ______.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. By the eighth week the gauge halfway down read no flow at all, and the gravel riffles between the river's deep bends lay dry and white in the sun. The bends, fed by seepage from shaded hillsides, kept their depth, and biologists netting them found trout crowded ten times thicker than in spring. Nearly all of those trout were alive when the autumn rains came. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: In 1965 a carmaker from abroad opened a plant outside a port city, on a site its board had chosen after two years of study. Behind a fence in the port's freight yard, it assembled two hundred cars a month from kits shipped in crates, and a single dealer in the city sold every one. When the government lifted its tariffs on foreign carmakers in 1970, the company built three full factories inland, staffed them with managers sent from abroad, and within a decade sold forty times as many cars. In a history of the company, one economist called the plant, above all, its ______ in the country.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: In 1980 a storm dropped a two-hundred-year-old fir into a mountain stream, and its trunk, four feet thick, has lain there ever since. It came to rest across the channel at water level, and each winter floods pour over it, scouring a pool on its downstream side and dropping the finer gravel in a broad bar below. Every autumn salmon dig their nests in that bar, and the young stay in the gravel until spring. Below the bar the stream spreads so shallow that deer wade it. After a decade of watching it, one ecologist called the log, above all, the valley's ______.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1987 a plowman near an old river landing turned up a clay pot buried around the year 900, holding some nine hundred silver coins and pieces of cut silver. The coins span forty years of local minting, the newest bright and the oldest worn smooth, except for a five-year gap that matches a famine recorded by a nearby abbey; the cut silver is old jewelry of the local style. The pot lay under the hearthstone of a farmhouse. From its contents, one archaeologist concluded that the hoard had been, above all, its owners' ______.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: In 1650 a printed collection brought to a mountain region a long tale, set in a distant desert capital, of a merchant's son who outwits a robber king. In the village versions recorded around 1900, the son had become the boy in the valley's legend of its patron saint, and the two stories' episodes alternated, all still set in the desert capital, with the robber king now beaten by the saint's prayer. A telling took twice as long as the printed text, and tellers disagreed about which episode came first. In a 1905 study, one folklorist argued that centuries of village retelling had, above all, ______ the tale.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: In the spring of 1952 a river in a dry farming valley flooded the lower fields, where irrigation had left a pale crust of salt. The water came down brown from hills burned bare the summer before, drained off within two days, and left dark silt a hand deep over the crust, with last year's stubble still poking through. That summer the same seed wheat that had always yielded half as much there as on the upper slopes outyielded them, and the gain shrank a little every harvest after. In a report on the valley's farms, one soil scientist wrote that the flood had ______ the lower fields.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Landing twenty years later, surveyors found bare rock, scored with grooves running downhill, where the farms and the village had been, and fishermen offshore still snagged roof beams and orchard stumps in their nets. The breakwater lay askew, its seaward end lower than its root, while every benchmark that survived on the island sat at its 1880 height. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. Radio stations had no reporters and read the papers' stories aloud only after the morning papers were on the street. Their programs made the same few comedians and commentators famous in every city, and the papers, finding those stars' columns sold best, bought them jointly through the wire service and let local writers go. By 1950 a reader opening the morning paper in any city met the same names. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: A rocky island a quarter mile long lies in the middle of a wide river where it crosses a farming valley. A stone wall rings its crown. When raiders came downriver in 1640 and again in 1702, the farms ferried their families and cattle over to it, and both times the raiders tried the wall for a day, then moved on. On either side the channel runs too deep to wade and too fast for a barge to tie up, and the river seldom rises more than a foot in spring. In a history of the valley, one historian called the island, above all, the valley's ______.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. Its staff sowed one strain of the district's usual wheat on the same plots, by the same methods, every year, and sold each harvest to a flour mill. Each autumn the county agent printed the station's yield per acre at the head of his report, and farms more than a fifth below it got a visit the next spring. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: A sand spit four miles long curves across a lagoon's mouth, with a lighthouse near its hooked tip and a road along its crest. In 1953 a three-day gale drove waves over the crest. Afterward the spit was as wide as before and its hooked tip lay where it had. The keeper, who had driven to town along the crest, now needed a boat. The lagoon's tide, which had always entered beside the tip, now arrived an hour sooner, and sooner each year after, while that old mouth sanded up. Comparing surveys made before and after that winter, one geologist concluded that the gale had ______ the spit.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: A gravel bar a mile long runs from the southern shore of a bay toward an island at the bay's mouth. Its far end meets a rock ledge that joins the island and never uncovers, even at the lowest tides. At high water barely three feet covers the crest, and storm swells pour over it into the bay. The town's flat-bottomed boats are hauled across on log rollers, and its houses are the only ones on that coast older than 1650, the year raiders sailed along it burning harbor towns. One historian of the bay's fishing town wrote that the bar had served the town above all as its ______.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: A cave opens in the side of a limestone hill above a village, and its passages wind back for a mile under the hill. Its mouth is its only opening, and the passages slope steeply down from it. In winter cold air pours in and settles, and ice that forms on the passage floors at midwinter lasts until the end of summer, when the drips melt it and it drains away through cracks in the floor. Until the 1950s the village kept its butter and meat there through the summer. In a survey of the district, one geologist called the cave, above all, the hill's ______.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: In a pond where half the snails carry a parasitic worm that matures inside ducks, a biologist kept infected and uninfected snails side by side for three years, in tanks and in a pen with feeding ducks. Infected snails grew slightly more slowly and laid slightly fewer eggs, and ducks in the pen took the two kinds at the same rate. In the second summer a bacterium swept the tanks, killing nine in ten uninfected snails and one in ten infected ones. From these results, she concluded that the worm had, above all, ______ its host.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: A cave high in a cliff overlooks a ford where reindeer herds crossed a river each spring and autumn fourteen thousand years ago; its back chamber stays near freezing all year. Just inside the mouth, a ledge faces straight down onto the ford. Excavators found it walled shut with stacked stones and, behind them, the uncut bones of twenty-three adults and children in layers spanning three thousand years, a reindeer antler laid across each layer. The hearths, tools and butchered reindeer bones of those centuries lie in camps by the river. From the finds, one archaeologist concluded that the valley's hunters used the cave above all as their ______.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: From 1950 to 1990, scientists studied one small, deep, cold lake in a northern forest more closely than any other lake in the region, and its bottom mud lies in fine yearly layers. Burrowing worms have churned the layers past reading, and its shrimp and plankton are those of every lake nearby. Scientists added acid to one basin of it and phosphate to the other, and the changes they measured were taken as what acid rain and farm runoff would do to the region's lakes. In a history of that work, one scientist called the lake, for those four decades, above all the region's ______.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. In 1608 a dispute over the festival calendar split the city temple's monks, and the smaller party, wanting the great festival at harvest rather than in spring, walked north and built on the hill. Its shrines follow the plain farmhouse style of the hills, and the city temple's abbot still names its head. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. The lake is three hundred feet deep, in a granite basin fed only by the river. Its outlet draws on cold water near the bottom, and the outflow rises and falls within a day of the inflow. Above the lake the river freezes in January and runs warm by August; the ponds have never frozen or failed. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. Along the shore the ice is frozen fast, thick and snow-covered, and does not move all winter, so almost nothing grows beneath it. Past its edge a lane of open water stays clear, and eiders and guillemots stand in rows along the edge between dives, plunging into the lane after fish. On the few days when gales pack the lane with drifting ice, the birds leave the bay. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay and a row of warehouses, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. In 1810 the cities built barracks on its heights and filled its warehouses with powder and grain. In three wars enemy fleets sailed past the island into the inland sea and took or burned port cities, and each time its garrison held out through a siege of months on what the warehouses held. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: A canal dug in the 1300s runs for two miles beside the old center of a river city. Low stone footbridges cross it every hundred yards, and houses from every quarter of the city face it from both its banks. Washerwomen worked its stone steps by day, crowds walked its paths on summer evenings, and in hard winters half the city skated on it. In her history of the city, one historian called the canal, above all, the city's ______.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: In 1838 a merchant inherited an estate of farms and oak woods worked by hired hands, and his account books for the next twenty years survive. From 1840 the hired hands' wages vanish from the books, and in their place, every autumn, come sums from some forty farm households, each the same from year to year. His son's inventory of 1858 lists the house, the farms and the oak woods as his father had found them. From those books, one historian concluded that, above all, he had ______ the estate.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: Between 1925 and 1935 a record company sent engineers into a mountain region to record its fiddlers and ballad singers, and it sold the records by the thousand. Within a decade nearly every farmhouse in the region had a phonograph, and families that had sung through the winter evenings sat and listened to the records instead; by 1950 few people there under forty could sing more than a line. The records kept every verse and every rough voice just as the engineers had found them. Looking back in 1970, one folklorist argued that the records had ______ the region's songs.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: In 1952, after three dry years, a river broke its banks and spread for five days across a broad valley, filling every side channel between its villages and their fields. When it drained, it did not go back to its old bed and kept instead a deep new channel it had cut down the valley's eastern side, which no ford or bridge crossed until 1963. The farmers all lived in villages on the western side, and the fields beyond the new channel, under a fresh layer of silt, went unsown for eleven years. One agronomist later argued that, for the farmers, the flood had above all ______ their fields.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. Because the museum planned to send the altarpiece on a ten-city tour, and the three panels together weighed four hundred pounds, the restorers faced the paint with tissue and shaved the sound oak away from behind it. They laid the paint layer, every brushstroke in place, onto light canvas stretched over aluminum frames, and left the darkened varnish for a later campaign. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: For six centuries an oasis of palms and wells stood alone on the caravan road across a desert, eleven days from the river and nine from the coast. Caravans from the river and from the coast both unloaded there, and merchants of a dozen peoples kept shops around its wells all year, buying from one caravan and selling to the next, so that few loads ever crossed the whole desert. Each caravan turned back from the oasis loaded with goods from the other end. In a history of the road, one scholar described the oasis as, above all, the desert's ______.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: For eighty years after 1890, companies mined copper from a mountain above a valley town, until the last mine closed in 1972. The ore lay in one great body under the summit, and from 1950 power shovels took it from above, bench by bench, the rock leaving by rail. The summit cairn of 1885 went in the first year, and the mountain now ends four hundred feet lower in a broad, flat shelf. Trout still rise in the streams that drain its slopes. Surveying the mountain in 1980, one geologist wrote that mining had ______ it.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
